paragraphs.text: For most of history, money was something that had value in itself. Coins of gold, silver or copper were worth roughly what their metal was worth, and a merchant who accepted them could, if necessary, melt them down and sell the metal. Clipping small pieces from the edges of coins was a common crime for exactly this reason. Paper money, by contrast, asks its holder to believe something. Paper money reversed this principle. A banknote is almost worthless as an object; its value rests entirely on the confidence of the people who use it that others will accept it in turn. How societies came to trust such a thing, and what happened when that trust failed, is one of the more remarkable stories in economic history, and it is far from finished.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first paper money appeared in China. In the eleventh century merchants in the province of Sichuan, where the local coins were made of heavy iron and were inconvenient to carry in large quantities, began depositing their coins with trusted agents and receiving paper certificates in return. The certificates circulated in place of the coins, and when the arrangement proved open to fraud, the state took it over and began issuing notes of its own. In the following centuries paper money came into use across much of China, and travellers from Europe described with astonishment a currency made from the bark of mulberry trees. Some visitors doubted that anyone would accept such a thing in exchange for real goods.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The Chinese experience also revealed the danger that has accompanied paper money ever since. Because notes cost almost nothing to produce, governments under financial pressure, particularly in wartime, were tempted to print more of them than the economy needed. As the quantity of notes grew faster than the goods available to buy, prices rose and the notes lost value. In the worst periods, notes that had once bought a meal would scarcely buy a handful of rice. By the fifteenth century the Chinese government had largely abandoned paper currency, and silver became the main medium of exchange. The lesson that the value of paper money depends on the discipline of those who issue it would be learned again, often painfully, in many other countries, and several modern states have repeated the experience.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: In Europe, paper money grew out of banking rather than out of government. Goldsmiths in seventeenth-century London, who kept customers’ gold in their vaults for safety, issued receipts to merchants who wanted to avoid carrying metal through dangerous streets. The receipts could be passed from hand to hand, and the goldsmiths soon discovered that they could issue more receipts than they held in gold, since depositors rarely all came to collect it at once. This practice allowed them to lend money and earn interest, but it also meant that a rumour of trouble could bring every depositor to the door at the same time. Banks that could not meet such demands collapsed, and their notes became worthless overnight. Such episodes did much to give banking a reputation for risk.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Over time, governments brought the issue of notes under control. National banks were given the sole right to issue them, and for much of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries many currencies were tied to gold: in principle, a holder could exchange a note for a fixed quantity of the metal at the issuing bank. The gold standard gave people confidence that notes would keep their value, but it also limited governments’ ability to respond to economic crises, since they could not increase the supply of money without increasing their gold reserves. During the twentieth century, one country after another abandoned the link, usually under the pressure of war or depression, when the need to spend outweighed the wish to keep the currency stable.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Today almost all money is what economists call fiat money, meaning that it has value because the state declares it to be the official means of payment and because people continue to accept it. Most of it does not exist as paper at all but as entries in bank accounts, and in several countries cash now accounts for only a small share of payments, and some shops no longer accept it at all. Central banks, which are usually independent of governments in their day-to-day decisions, are responsible for keeping inflation low, largely to preserve the confidence on which the whole system rests.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The history of paper money is often told as a story of progress from the solid to the abstract, but it can also be read as a series of experiments in trust, and every stage has been accompanied by doubts, many of which proved justified. Each new form of money, from the merchant’s certificate to the electronic payment, has depended on people believing that a promise will be kept. When that belief is strong, money can take almost any form; when it collapses, as it has during periods of extreme inflation, people abandon the official currency and turn to foreign coins, precious metals or the simple exchange of goods. The material of money, in the end, has always mattered less than the confidence behind it.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: At its greatest extent, the Roman Empire was connected by a network of more than eighty thousand kilometres of paved roads, stretching from northern Britain to the edge of the Arabian desert. Distances along them were measured in Roman miles, each of a thousand paces. Many of these roads are still visible, and some still carry traffic, their routes followed by modern motorways. They were not the first roads in the ancient world, but no earlier state had built so many to so consistent a standard, and none had used them so deliberately as instruments of power. For archaeologists, they offer an unusual opportunity: a single system, built over several centuries, whose remains can be traced across dozens of modern countries. Some have been excavated in detail, while others are known only from maps and inscriptions.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The roads were built first for the army. As Rome expanded through Italy and then beyond it, new roads were laid out to allow legions to reach frontier regions quickly and to be supplied once they were there. The earliest major road, begun in the late fourth century BC, ran south from Rome and was named after the official who ordered it, and it was paved along its whole length, an extraordinary undertaking at the time. Later roads followed conquering armies into Gaul, Spain and the eastern provinces. Soldiers did much of the construction themselves, and a legion stationed in a quiet province might spend years building roads rather than fighting. The roads also carried a message: wherever they ran, Rome’s authority ran with them.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Roman engineers favoured straight lines wherever the terrain allowed. Surveyors used simple instruments, including a device made of weighted strings hanging from a cross, to lay out long straight sections between high points from which signal fires could be seen. Where a straight route was impossible, roads zigzagged up hillsides or were cut into rock, and bridges and tunnels carried them across rivers and through ridges. Some of the stone bridges built for these roads are still in use two thousand years later, a testament less to any secret method than to careful construction and generous proportions. Engineers were not afraid of steep gradients, and some roads climbed slopes that later wagon drivers found exhausting.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: A typical major road was built in layers. Workers dug a trench down to firm ground and filled it with successive layers of large stones, smaller stones and gravel mixed with lime or sand, before laying a surface of closely fitted paving slabs or compacted gravel, so that the total depth could exceed a metre. The surface was slightly curved so that rainwater ran off into ditches on either side, and in many places kerbstones held the edges in place. This layered structure spread the weight of heavy wagons and allowed the road to drain, which is why so many sections have survived centuries of neglect. Minor roads were far simpler, often little more than gravel tracks.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The roads carried far more than soldiers. Officials, messengers and merchants used them, and a state postal service maintained stations at regular intervals where official travellers could change horses and find lodging, and a messenger changing horses frequently could cover well over a hundred kilometres in a day. Milestones recorded the distance to the nearest town and often the name of the emperor responsible for the road’s construction or repair, so that the stones served as advertisements of imperial generosity as well as guides for travellers. Some milestones have since been found far from their original positions, reused in walls and churches. Towns grew up at road junctions and river crossings, and many modern European cities trace their origins to such places, where inns, shops and workshops followed the traffic.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Historians have debated how much the roads contributed to the empire’s economy. Transport by land was slow and expensive compared with transport by water: moving heavy goods a few hundred kilometres by wagon could double their price, while ships carried grain across the Mediterranean far more cheaply, and rivers and canals were used wherever they existed. Some scholars therefore argue that the roads mattered mainly for administration and for the movement of people and information, and that bulky trade continued to depend on seas and rivers. Others point out that roads connected inland areas to ports and made local markets possible where no water route existed. The answer probably differed from one province to another.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: After the western empire collapsed in the fifth century, the roads were no longer maintained by any central authority. Their surfaces decayed, stones were removed for building, and in many places the routes were abandoned in favour of tracks that followed more convenient local paths; some sections vanished beneath fields and forests. Yet the network left a lasting mark. Medieval travellers still used many Roman routes, boundaries between parishes and counties often follow their lines, and archaeologists using aerial photographs and laser scanning continue to discover lost sections, adding to the map of a system that, in its scale and ambition, would not be matched in Europe until the railways of the nineteenth century. Many modern travellers use its routes without knowing it.
paragraphs.label: G

texts.title: Should pupils be grouped by ability?

paragraphs.text: In many schools, children of the same age are divided into groups according to their perceived ability, either for all subjects or for particular ones such as mathematics, and its forms vary from country to country. The practice goes by different names: streaming when pupils are placed in the same group for everything, setting when they are grouped separately for each subject, and tracking in the United States. Its supporters say it allows teachers to pitch lessons at the right level for everyone. Its critics say it fixes children’s futures too early and widens the gaps it is meant to address. Few questions in education produce such confident claims on both sides, and such mixed evidence. Both sides can point to research that supports them.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The case for grouping is intuitive. A teacher facing thirty pupils whose knowledge of fractions ranges from none to complete mastery cannot easily teach all of them at once; the most advanced will be bored and the least advanced lost. Teachers themselves often favour grouping for this reason. The education researcher Helen Clarke argues that grouping allows teachers to move faster with pupils who are ready and to spend more time on basics with those who need it. Her own studies found that the highest-attaining pupils made modestly faster progress in set classes than in mixed ones, particularly in mathematics and foreign languages. The gains were small, however, and Clarke does not claim that lower groups benefit.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The difficulty is that the gains for the highest groups appear to be matched, or outweighed, by losses for the lowest. The sociologist Martin Reyes, who has reviewed decades of studies, concludes that pupils placed in low groups tend to make less progress than similar pupils taught in mixed classes, partly because they are often given less experienced teachers and less demanding work. He accepts that the effects vary between subjects and ages. Expectations matter too. When a pupil is placed in a bottom group, teachers, parents and the pupil may all come to see that position as a measure of ability rather than of current attainment, and act accordingly. Pupils, too, may lower their own expectations once they know which group they are in.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: A further concern is how pupils are allocated in the first place. Placement decisions are meant to be based on attainment, but studies in several countries have found that pupils from poorer families and those born late in the school year are more likely to be placed in lower groups than their test results alone would predict. Reyes argues that this makes grouping a mechanism for reproducing existing inequalities rather than responding to individual needs. Once placed, moreover, pupils rarely move: one large study found that most of those assigned to a group at the age of seven were still in the same group years later. Some schools test pupils only once, at entry, and changing groups can also mean changing friends, which many pupils resist.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Defenders of grouping reply that these are problems of practice, not of principle; the idea, in other words, is sound even if its application is often poor. If allocation were based strictly on current attainment, if movement between groups were regular and if the best teachers were assigned to the lowest groups rather than the highest, many of the harmful effects might disappear. The headteacher and writer Samuel Owusu describes a school that reorganised its sets in exactly this way, reviewing every pupil’s placement each term and giving the weakest groups the smallest classes. Results improved across the school, though he is careful to add that other changes were made at the same time. He also acknowledges that the arrangement demanded a great deal of the school’s most experienced staff.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Mixed-ability teaching has its own difficulties. It requires teachers to plan work that can be approached at different levels, which is demanding and time-consuming, and done badly it can leave the most able pupils coasting. Teachers in mixed classes also report that preparing several versions of each task is exhausting. The psychologist Anna Lindqvist, who has studied how pupils feel about their placement, found that many pupils in mixed classes were acutely aware of who was struggling and who was not, so that grouping within a single class could be as visible, and as discouraging, as separate sets. Simply abolishing sets, she suggests, does not remove comparison between pupils. Pupils notice differences, whatever the timetable says.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: My own view is that the evidence does not support grouping by ability as it is usually practised, particularly for young children, but that it does not support a blanket ban either, or the certainty with which each side states its case. Where schools use sets, they should base them on recent evidence of attainment, review them often and give the lowest groups their best teaching rather than their least. Where they teach mixed classes, they need to give teachers the time and training to make them work. The question that matters is not whether pupils are grouped but whether every group is expected, and helped, to learn. That is a harder question, and a more useful one.
paragraphs.label: G
